name: Epiphanius of Salamis
otherNames: Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia in Cyprus
knownFor: Bishop of Salamis in Cyprus, author of the Panarion against the heresies, and a leading accuser of Origen in the quarrels of the 390s and early 400s.
dates: Born about 310, bishop about 368 or 369, died in 403 (Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to the Lives of Illustrious Men by Jerome of Strido)
place: Born at Besauduc near Eleutheropolis in Palestine; bishop at Salamis, also called Constantia, in Cyprus

keyWorks.title: Panarion
keyWorks.about: his book against the heresies, which Jerome calls "Against all heresies"; heresies 34 to 80 are held in Greek

keyWorks.title: Ancoratus
keyWorks.about: "The Anchored", which the monk Ammonius says in Sozomen's account he had read often; not held in the Library

keyWorks.title: Letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem
keyWorks.about: his defence of the ordination of Paulinian and his charges against Origen, held in Jerome's Latin version, in English

traces: The Panarion's account of the heresies. It keeps writings of some of those it attacks, among them the propositions of Aetius of Antioch, quoted in heresy 76.
The condemnation of Origen's books in Cyprus, which Socrates of Constantinople and Sozomen say he decreed at a synod there.
remembered: Sozomen calls him "the most revered man under the whole heaven", and says it was reported that demons were driven out and diseases healed at his tomb.
Jerome says his books were read by the learned for their matter, "and also by the plain people, on account of their language."
Socrates of Constantinople says that "on account of his extraordinary piety" he was "a man of simple mind and manners", and that Theophilus of Alexandria used him.

uncertain: Epiphanius wrote against the heresies as their enemy, and his reports of them are a foe's.
Socrates and Sozomen report his last words to John Chrysostom, and John's answer, as hearsay. Socrates says he cannot be sure his informants spoke the truth.

Theophilus of Alexandria once accused him of thinking that God has a human form, Socrates says. A. C. Zenos, in a note to his translation of Socrates, says Epiphanius himself rejected that view, on Jerome's testimony.

Theophilus's own judgment of him changed. The Dialogue on the life of Chrysostom, which Herbert Moore gives to Palladius of Helenopolis, says Theophilus first called him "a heretic, or a paltry schismatic", and later "a most holy saint".
His dates are Richardson's reckoning. No held ancient source gives the year of his birth.
The Library holds the Panarion only from heresy 34 on, in Greek, and the Ancoratus not at all.
